lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- Checkpoint: Ten Days, One Trip
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Patrícia Yamaguti | Lesson 10 -- Checkpoint

listenings.text: Good morning, and welcome to your last day with us. This message is for the guests who leave today. Check-out is at eleven, and if you need one more hour, just call the reception. You can leave your bags in the small room next to the desk, and take them in the afternoon. Breakfast is until ten, on the ground floor, and today we have fruit and warm bread. If you need a taxi to the airport, call us thirty minutes before, and remember that on Sunday the traffic is slow, so leave early. One last thing: please check the room before you go, because every week somebody leaves a passport or a phone in the safe. It is a long way back. Thank you for staying with us, and have a very good trip home.

And now our travel minute. This week we talked to families about the first trip abroad with small children, and one answer came back again and again. It was not the money, and it was not the flight. It was the language. One mother told us she did not go into a single shop in ten days, because she was afraid of the moment somebody asks a question. Our expert says the same thing every time: you do not need to understand every word. You need three sentences. The first one asks people to repeat. The second one asks them to speak more slowly. And the third one asks for help. With those three, she says, a person who knows two hundred words can travel anywhere in the world. And that is our travel minute. Have a good week.

extra_audio.text: Sorry, I don't understand. Can you say that again, please? Can you speak more slowly? I am lost. Can you help me, please? Thank you very much.

reading.rtitle: Ten Days -- a page from a travel diary
paras: Day one. The airport at seven in the morning, two children and three bags. I gave my ticket and my passport, I asked where the gate was, and I understood the answer. On the plane I ordered the chicken, and I told the crew that my son is allergic to nuts. Nobody ordered for me.

Day two. The officer asked why I was here and how long I stay. Two weeks, I said, and the address of the hotel. Thirty seconds, and we were in. At the hotel there were no towels, so I called the reception and asked them to send someone. Four towels, ten minutes.

Day four. I went into a store alone, with the children. I pointed at a dress and asked how much it was. Forty-five pounds. I asked for another color, I tried it on, and I said the shoes were too expensive for me. I walked out with one bag and without my husband.

Day six. We had dinner for four people, and I ordered everything: a salad, two pasta, one fish and some bread. Day eight, I was lost in the street with no battery on my phone, and a man showed me the way on his map. I repeated it back to be sure, and I got to the hotel. Day nine, the dress was too tight, so I went back and exchanged it. They said no to the money, and I asked for a bigger size instead. Ten days, and I spoke in every one of them.
